title: Coordinate Parser: Messy Strings to Clean Values
description: Turn a pasted coordinate string into clean latitude and longitude values with the Coordinate Parser — separators, symbols and all. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, '40°45′28.8″N, 73°59′07.8″W' pasted from a PDF becomes 40.7580, −73.9855 — the same point, with the typography stripped away.
quick_answer: The Coordinate Parser turns a pasted coordinate string into clean latitude and longitude values for further mapping work. Paste the string — symbols, letters, odd separators and all — and read the two numbers, parsed and range-checked, ready for converters, maps and forms that want plain values.

Coordinates hide in message threads in every dress imaginable — the parser's tolerance is built from those threads' greatest hits.

Smart quotes, prime symbols and a non-breaking space walk into a paste. The parser reads through them to the numbers — 40.7580, −73.9855 — because coordinates should survive copy-paste.
'40.7580 N, 73.9855 W' parses to signed decimals: letters fold into signs (W negative), once, without the double-negation trap.

faq: What separators work?
Commas, spaces, semicolons and the usual symbol sets — the parser is liberal in what it accepts and strict in what it returns: two validated numbers.
Does it geocode the point?
No — parsing extracts coordinates from text; it does not look the place up. The Reverse Geocoder and City from Coordinates tools do the looking-up.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
Parsing is datum-neutral; the site's working datum is WGS84, which parsed GPS strings almost always are.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
The parser preserves the digits you give it — preservation is not endorsement. The precision tools judge what the digits are worth.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Yes — clean signed decimals are every GIS's native tongue.
Swapped lat/lon in my string?
Range checks catch impossible swaps (a 'latitude' of −122). Plausible swaps need context — the detector's continent test is the second opinion.
European decimal commas?
A known trap (40,7580) — the parser's handling distinguishes decimal commas from pair separators by structure; when honestly ambiguous, it says so.
UTM or grid strings?
Grid values are a different family — the MGRS, BNG and Irish helpers convert those; the parser's domain is lat/lon dresses.
Batch strings?
One string per parse here. Columns of strings belong to the Batch Geocoder's world or a script — spot-check their output here.
It failed to parse.
Read the flag: out-of-range values, missing components and address-like text each fail differently, and the failure message is the diagnosis.
Leading plus signs and trailing zeros?
Both parse cleanly — cosmetics the parser absorbs without comment.
